bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: The two-step bucket dance: create-if-missing, then push. Unlike indexBy, repeated keys ACCUMULATE instead of overwriting — the structural difference between an index and a grouping.
hints: Ensure the bucket array exists, then push.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `countBy` that counts records per value of `record[key]` (args: records, key): `([{s:"open"},{s:"open"},{s:"done"}], "s")` → `{ open: 2, done: 1 }`.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: countBy is groupBy that keeps only the bucket sizes — when the report needs numbers, skip storing the records. Status-badge counts in every dashboard sidebar are a countBy.
hints: Like groupBy, but accumulate a number instead of an array.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `totalsBy` that sums `record[valueKey]` per value of `record[groupKey]` (args: records, groupKey, valueKey): totals per category.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: Swap the `+ 1` of countBy for `+ r[valueKey]` and counting becomes summing — the same accumulate-into-buckets skeleton underlies count, sum, min, max and average by group. This IS GROUP BY SUM from SQL.
hints: countBy, but add the value field instead of 1.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `namesById` that builds a lean lookup: maps each record’s `id` to just its `name` (not the whole record) from `{ id, name, ... }` records.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: The value side of an index is a choice: whole record when you need everything, a single field when you need one. Lean id→name maps are what UIs use to render labels for foreign keys without dragging full records around.
hints: Index build, but store r.name as the value.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `idSet` that builds a fast membership lookup: maps each record’s `id` to `true` from `{ id, ... }` records, so callers can test `set[id]`.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: When only is-it-there matters, the value degenerates to true and the object acts as a set: `seen[id]` is a constant-time membership test. (A real Set does this too; the object form composes with JSON and spreads.)
hints: The value is just true — presence is the point.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `cheapestByCategory` that maps each category to the LOWEST price among records `{ category, price }` (args: records).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: Min-per-group is the bucket skeleton holding a champion instead of a count: first occurrence seeds the bucket (hasOwn), later ones only overwrite when smaller. Price-comparison pages and "best score per level" tables are this loop.
hints: Write when the key is new OR the price beats the stored one.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `distinctValuesOf` that returns the distinct values of `record[key]` across an array of records, in first-seen order (args: records, key).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: Projection then dedupe: map narrows records to the one field, the Set spread removes repeats. Populating a filter dropdown with the statuses that actually occur in the data is this exact line.
hints: map out the field, Set-dedupe the result.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `namesByTeam` that groups records `{ team, name }` into an object mapping team → array of NAMES (not whole records).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: Grouping and projecting can happen in the same pass: the bucket collects just the field the consumer needs. Roster views — team → member names — skip carrying full records through.
hints: groupBy, but push r.name instead of r.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export a function `averageByLevel` that returns the mean score per level from records `{ level, score }` — track sums and counts, then divide (test data divides evenly).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: An average cannot be accumulated directly — it is a ratio of two accumulable quantities. Track sum and count per bucket, divide at the end. Any "running average" scheme that skips this decomposition drifts wrong.
hints: Averages need TWO accumulators per group: sum and count.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions:
Export `attachAuthors(posts, users)` where posts are `{ title, authorId }` and users are `{ id, name }`.
Return a new array of `{ title, authorName }`, using `'unknown'` when the authorId matches no user.
Build a users index FIRST — do not call find inside the loop.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: This is a JOIN: the index turns the O(posts × users) nested-find approach into O(posts + users) — build the lookup once, then map with constant-time access. The `?.name ?? 'unknown'` chain handles the dangling foreign key, the data equivalent of a LEFT JOIN with a default.
hints: Index users by id once; then each post is a single lookup.
A miss reads as undefined — ?. plus ?? turns it into "unknown".

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions: Export `firstBy(records, key)` returning an object mapping each distinct `record[key]` to the FIRST record having it (later duplicates must NOT overwrite).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: indexBy with the write guarded: existing entries are never overwritten, so the first occurrence wins (plain indexBy keeps the LAST). First-wins vs last-wins is a one-line difference with real consequences — deduplicating signups, earliest event per user, etc.
hints: Only write when the key is not already present — hasOwn guard.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.instructions:
Export `stockLevels(movements)` where each movement is `{ sku, type, qty }` with type `'in'` or `'out'` (qty positive).
Return an object mapping each sku to its net stock (in minus out) — but EXCLUDE skus whose net is 0 from the result entirely.
`stockLevels([{sku:'a',type:'in',qty:5},{sku:'a',type:'out',qty:5}])` → `{}`
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/lo.explanation: Two shaping phases: an accumulate-by-key pass (totalsBy with signed deltas), then an object filter to drop the zero rows — the entries/fromEntries sandwich from the objects module. Note negative nets survive: oversold stock is information, and only exact zero means "nothing to report". Event streams folded into current state is how ledgers, carts and game inventories actually work.
hints: Accumulate signed deltas per sku: in → +qty, out → -qty.
The zero-filter is the entries→filter→fromEntries sandwich.
Filter on v !== 0, not truthiness… actually !== 0 and truthiness agree here — but !== 0 says what you mean.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: The callback writes through the shared reference, so every original row is modified, and `out` holds the very same objects — any other code reading `rows` sees trimmed names. Build new objects instead: (r) => ({ ...r, name: r.name.trim() }).

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Destructure-in-parameter projection: only the named fields enter the new object, so secretCost never reaches the output (false) while the source still has it (true). Allowlist projection like this is how APIs avoid leaking internal fields.
hints: The destructuring picks three fields; secretCost is simply never copied.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `toOptions` that maps records `{ id, name, ... }` to `<select>`-style options `{ value, label }` where value is the id and label the name.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Projection with renaming: the destination (a dropdown component) dictates the field names, the map adapts to them. Extra source fields vanish because the new literal never mentions them.
hints: map to fresh two-field objects.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `withTotals` that enriches order lines `{ qty, priceCents }` by ADDING a `totalCents` field (qty × priceCents), keeping all existing fields; do not mutate the inputs.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Enrichment: `{ ...l, totalCents }` copies the row and adds one derived field — the originals stay pristine (spread, not assignment). Derived fields computed at the edge beat storing them, which risks going stale.
hints: Spread the line, append the computed field.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `toApiShape` that converts internal records `{ userName, userEmail }` to API shape `{ name, email }`.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Boundary translation: internal naming conventions rarely match the wire format, so a mapping layer renames explicitly. Keeping it in one function means the rename exists in exactly one place.
hints: Destructure the old names, emit the new ones.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `overdueTitles` that from tasks `{ title, daysLate, done }`: the TITLES of unfinished tasks with daysLate > 0, sorted most-late first (include daysLate in the sort, return titles only; args: tasks).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Order of operations is the lesson: sorting must happen BEFORE the map strips daysLate away — after projection the sort key is gone. Filter-sort-project is the standard list-view pipeline.
hints: filter → sort (while you still have daysLate!) → map.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `orderLines` that flattens orders `{ orderId, items: [{ sku, qty }] }` into one row per item: `{ orderId, sku, qty }` (flatMap).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Denormalization: each child row gets its parent’s id stamped on (spread after the explicit field would also work — here item has no orderId to clash). Nested-to-flat is how you prep data for tables and CSV exports.
hints: flatMap over orders; inner map stamps the parent id onto each item.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `orderSummary` that aggregates order lines `{ totalCents }` into `{ count, totalCents, maxCents }` (zeros for an empty array).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Aggregation does not require one reduce per statistic: a single pass updates all the accumulators together. count/sum/max in one loop is both faster and — once you read it as "one pass, three facts" — clearer than three chained methods.
hints: One loop can feed several accumulators at once.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `normalizeEmails` that maps records `{ email, ... }` to new records with the email trimmed and lower-cased, all other fields preserved.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Cleaning on the way in: spread-and-override normalizes one field without disturbing the rest. Normalizing emails before comparing or storing prevents the duplicate-account-with-different-casing bug.
hints: Spread the record, override just email.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `priceBands` that maps products `{ name, cents }` to `{ name, band }` where band is `'budget'` below 1000, `'mid'` from 1000 to 4999, `'premium'` at 5000+.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Transformations can embed logic: the map callback runs a threshold chain per row and emits a projected object carrying the computed label. Bucketing continuous values into named bands is standard prep for display and grouping.
hints: Classify inside the map callback, then build the projection.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `topScorers` that returns the `n` highest-scoring names from records `{ name, score }`, highest first (args: records, n); do not mutate the input.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: The top-N pipeline: copy (sort mutates), order, truncate, project — in that order, because slicing before sorting takes the wrong rows and projecting before sorting discards the sort key. Leaderboards, "top products", trending lists: all this pipeline.
hints: Copy → sort desc → slice n → project names.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `dedupeById` that removes records with duplicate `id`s, keeping the FIRST occurrence and preserving order (args: records).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Objects defeat the Set-spread trick (identity comparison), so dedupe goes key-based: a seen lookup remembers processed ids and gates the output push. Merging API pages that overlap at the boundary needs exactly this.
hints: A seen-set guards the push; Set-spread cannot dedupe objects.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions: Export a function `partitionByStock` that splits products `{ name, stock }` into `{ inStock, soldOut }` — two arrays of names, by stock > 0.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: Partition: both halves in one pass, with the ternary selecting the destination array (two filters would also work — at two scans). Splitting a list into shown/hidden, valid/invalid, paid/unpaid is a daily occurrence.
hints: One pass; the ternary picks which array receives the push.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions:
Export `toCsv(records, columns)` where `columns` is an array of key names.
Return an array of strings: first a header line of the column names joined by commas, then one line per record with the column values joined by commas (missing values become empty strings).
`toCsv([{a:1,b:2}], ['a','b'])` → `['a,b', '1,2']`
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: The inner map runs over `columns`, not Object.keys(record) — that single choice guarantees column order, includes empty cells for missing keys (`?? ''`), and ignores extra fields. Driving output shape from a spec list rather than from the data is a transferable reporting pattern.
hints: The header is just columns joined.
Each row: map the COLUMNS (not the record keys) so order and gaps are controlled.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions:
Export `paginate(records, page, perPage)` (page is 1-based) returning
`{ items, page, totalPages }` where totalPages is `Math.ceil(records.length / perPage)` (minimum 1).
Pages beyond the end return an empty items array.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: The (page − 1) × perPage conversion between human 1-based pages and 0-based indexes is where most pagination bugs live. slice forgives out-of-range pages with an empty result, and the Math.max floor means even an empty collection reports page 1 of 1 — UI code downstream appreciates never seeing page 1 of 0.
hints: start index: (page - 1) × perPage — the 1-based to 0-based shift.
slice past the end harmlessly yields [].
Math.max(1, ...) keeps totalPages sensible for empty data.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.instructions:
Export `salesReport(sales)` where each sale is `{ region, product, cents }`.
Return an array of per-region summaries, one object per distinct region:
`{ region, totalCents, saleCount, topProduct }`
- topProduct: the product with the highest cents-sum WITHIN that region (ties: alphabetically first product wins)
- the result array sorted by totalCents descending (ties: region ascending alphabetically)
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/tr.explanation: A genuine report pipeline: one accumulation pass builds nested state (per-region totals plus a per-product sub-tally), then an entries→map→sort pass shapes it for presentation. Both the topProduct pick and the final ordering reuse the `primary || tiebreak` comparator chain. Nested grouping like this — group, then aggregate within each group — is the shape of virtually every analytics endpoint.
hints: Phase 1: accumulate per region — totals, counts, and a nested per-product sum object.
Phase 2: entries → map each region to its summary, picking topProduct from the nested sums.
Both orderings use the comparator-chain trick: primary || tiebreak.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: React re-renders when `newState !== oldState` (reference check). Why does `state.count++; setState(state)` fail to update the UI?
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: Mutation changes contents, not identity: the object passed back IS the old object, so `newState === oldState` and the framework concludes nothing happened. A new object — { ...state, count: state.count + 1 } — changes the reference and triggers the render.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Which of these does NOT mutate the array it is called on?
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: filter builds a new array of the keepers; the original is untouched. push, sort and splice all modify in place — the mutators to avoid (or to call only on a fresh copy) when working immutably.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Read the code below and predict exactly what it prints.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: The settings branch was rebuilt (new object, theme dark; old keeps light; references differ → false). The user branch was NOT on the changed path, so it rides along by reference (true). Copy the changed path, share the rest — structural sharing in four lines.
hints: Which branch was spread (copied) and which was merely referenced?

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `setField` that returns a new object: `obj` with `field` (a fixed key passed as a string) set to `value` (args: obj, field, value); input untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: The fundamental immutable write: copy everything, override one computed key. Every state-management library’s "set" is this line with bookkeeping around it.
hints: Spread + computed key.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `dropField` that returns a new object without `field` (args: obj, field) — use destructuring with a COMPUTED key: `const { [field]: _, ...rest } = obj`.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: The computed-key pattern `{ [field]: removed, ...rest }` extracts a dynamically-named property; `rest` is the object without it. Dropping an absent field just copies — no error, no phantom key.
hints: Computed keys work in destructuring patterns too.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `addTodo` that returns a new array with `{ id, text, done: false }` appended to `todos` (args: todos, id, text); input untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: Immutable append with the new record built inline — property shorthand for id and text, a fixed default for done. The old array is never touched, so undo/redo and change detection keep working.
hints: Spread the old list; the new object literal goes last.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `removeTodo` that returns a new array without the todo whose `id` matches (args: todos, id); other elements keep their identity.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: filter IS immutable removal: survivors pass through by reference (cheap), the match is simply absent from the new array. A no-match id removes nothing and still returns a fresh array.
hints: filter with !== keeps everything except the target.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `toggleTodo` that returns a new array where the todo with matching `id` has `done` flipped, everything else untouched (args: todos, id).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: THE recipe: map visits all, the ternary rebuilds only the match ({ ...t, done: !t.done }) and returns every other element unchanged — same reference. One new array, one new element, maximal sharing.
hints: map + ternary: copy-with-change for the match, pass-through otherwise.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `renameUser` that returns a new array of users `{ id, name }` where the user with matching `id` gets `name` replaced by `newName` (args: users, id, newName).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: toggleTodo with the change swapped: the recipe is field-agnostic. Once map-ternary-spread is muscle memory, every "update record X in list" task is a fill-in-the-blanks exercise.
hints: Same map-ternary recipe, different field.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `incrementStat` that given state `{ stats: { clicks, views }, ...other }`, returns a new state with `stats[statName]` incremented by 1 (args: state, statName); copy only the changed path.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: A two-level immutable update: each level on the path to the change gets its own spread, the computed key targets the stat, and untouched siblings (views, user) are carried by the spreads. Count the spreads: exactly as many as levels changed — no more.
hints: Two spreads: the root and the stats branch; computed key inside.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `markAllDone` that returns a new array where EVERY todo `{ id, done }` gets `done: true` — new objects for all elements, input untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: When every element changes, the ternary drops away: map plus spread-override rebuilds each one. "Mark all read", "select all", "archive all" — the bulk version of the single-item recipe.
hints: map with spread-override — no ternary needed when all change.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `stripPasswords` that returns a new array of users with the `password` property removed from each (rest destructuring in the callback), inputs untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: The immutable field-removal recipe mapped over a list, with the destructuring done in the callback’s parameter — password is bound (and ignored) and rest is the clean copy. Sanitizing a collection before res.json(...) is this one-liner.
hints: Destructure password away right in the parameter.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `swapItems` that returns a new array with the elements at indexes `i` and `j` exchanged (args: arr, i, j); input untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: Copy-then-mutate-the-copy is a legitimate immutable strategy: the spread isolates the caller’s array, after which in-place tricks (the destructuring swap) are safe. Reordering items in a drag-and-drop list uses this shape.
hints: Copy first, then the destructuring swap on the copy.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `addTag` that given state `{ tags: [...], ...other }`, returns a new state with `tag` appended to tags — but UNCHANGED (same object is fine) if the tag is already present (args: state, tag).
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: Two ideas at once: a no-op returns the ORIGINAL state (cheap, and frameworks skip re-rendering), and a real change copies both the root and the array level. Spread the object, spread the array — the list is part of the changed path.
hints: Guard with includes; otherwise spread both levels.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export a function `insertSorted` that returns a new array with `n` inserted into an already-ascending array of numbers at its correct position (args: sorted, n); input untouched.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: findIndex finds the insertion point (first element greater than n); the two-slice sandwich from insertAt places the value there. The -1 branch (nothing larger) appends. Keeping a list sorted on insert beats re-sorting the world each time.
hints: findIndex locates the first larger element; -1 means append.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions:
Export `markDone(todos, id)` returning a new array where the matching todo gets `done: true`.
The tests verify THREE identity facts: the array is new, the changed element is new, and UNCHANGED elements are the very same objects as before.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: The identity tests pin down what "immutable update" precisely means: new array (change detectable), new changed element, SAME untouched elements (so memoized children skip re-rendering). A deep clone would pass the value tests but fail the sharing test — over-copying is a real performance bug, not just a style issue.
hints: The map-ternary recipe does all three automatically.
Deep-cloning everything would FAIL the identity test on unchanged elements.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions: Export `newestFirst(posts)` where posts are `{ title, day }` (day: number). Return a NEW array sorted by day descending without mutating the input.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: sort is on the mutators list, so immutable code always gives it a fresh copy to chew on: `[...posts].sort(...)`. (The newer `posts.toSorted(...)` does copy+sort in one call.) Forgetting the spread here is the single most common immutability slip in review.
hints: Copy before sorting — sort mutates its receiver.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.instructions:
Export `cartReducer(state, action)` — a pure function over `{ items: [{ sku, qty }], coupon: string|null }`:
- `{ type: 'add', sku }`: if the sku exists, increment its qty (immutably); else append `{ sku, qty: 1 }`
- `{ type: 'remove', sku }`: remove the item entirely
- `{ type: 'setCoupon', code }`: set coupon to `code`
- `{ type: 'clear' }`: return `{ items: [], coupon: null }`
- unknown type: return `state` UNCHANGED (same reference!)
Never mutate `state` or anything inside it.
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/im.explanation: This is the exact contract of a Redux/useReducer reducer: pure, immutable, and — the subtle requirement — returning the SAME reference for no-op actions, so the framework can skip re-rendering entirely. Every branch composes recipes you drilled: map-ternary increment, filter removal, spread override, and the some() existence check choosing between update and append.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/ne.explanation: Each ?. guards only its own link. In `o.a?.b.c`, the guard sits on reading b (fine — a exists), but then `.c` is a PLAIN access on `o.a.b`, which is undefined → TypeError. Option C survives because ?.c guards the read on the undefined b. Guard every link that can be absent.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/ne.explanation: The recursion mirrors the spread pyramid exactly: each call copies one level and delegates the remainder of the path, and the empty-path base case bottoms out by returning the new value. Walking it for a 3-key path produces precisely the three nested spreads you wrote by hand in setCity — recursion is how the pattern generalizes to any depth.

Otherwise: spread this level, and recurse for the [head] key with the rest of the path.
head/rest come from array destructuring: const [head, ...rest] = path.

bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/ne.instructions:
Export `summarizeResponse(res)` for a loosely-shaped API response that MAY look like:
`{ data: { user: { name, orders: [{ total }] } }, error: { message } }`
— but any branch can be missing, and `res` itself can be null.
Return:
- `{ ok: false, message }` when there is an error message (`res.error.message`), using message `'request failed'` if error exists but has no message
- otherwise `{ ok: true, name, orderCount, grandTotal }` where name defaults to `'anonymous'`, orders default to `[]`, and grandTotal sums the `total` fields (missing totals count as 0)
bootforge/arrays-objects/data-shaping/ne.explanation: Defensive reading at scale: the error guard runs first (with its own inner default), then every data access is guarded (`?.`) and defaulted (`??`) at the right granularity — the array as a whole, then each total within the reduce. Defaulting `orders` to `[]` is the pivotal move: it lets length and reduce run unconditionally. This function is the shape of every "render an API response without crashing" utility you will ever write.
hints: Error branch first — it preempts everything else.
Default the ARRAY (?? []) before reducing, and default each total inside the reduce.
Every read from res goes through ?. — res itself can be null.
